speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I thank the Minister Desmond Lee for his first Motion speech; I will deliver the second one.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I clarify that your Motion has two points?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, I said you can ask your clarifications later.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government's Motion, on the other hand, suggests that there is no need to review its current housing policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: PSP will state our position clearly and I hope that the Government will also state clearly why it thinks that public housing is still affordable and accessible today, and against whom is it protecting the interests of the current and future generations of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is clear that the Government is not confident that Singaporeans believe in its housing policies since the Government has been running extensive advertisements in the mainstream media to illustrate the affordability of BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If HDB flats are truly affordable and accessible, Singaporeans will know it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If Singaporeans are not satisfied, the Government should be proactively reviewing its policies and telling Singaporeans what corrective actions it will be taking to resolve housing problems.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Minister has covered some of the corrective policy actions that the Government is going to take, but I think that is not all.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Singaporeans should be treated like citizens, not consumers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: During the early years of Independence, when land cost was not built into the price of a HDB flat, the Government was able to provide a roof over the heads of all Singaporeans who needed it, in a timely manner and at affordable prices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The security of a stable dwelling liberated Singaporeans in that generation and provided them with the energy to build a new nation and change Singapore for the better.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, the situation changed drastically in the 1990s, when the Government started to treat HDB flats as an appreciating asset.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In 1995, then Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong told Singaporeans that we are embarking on "a new phase where the Government increases your asset value through the Asset Enhancement Programme".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As a result, the heavy burden of home ownership today robs young Singaporeans of the financial security they need to be enterprising risk-takers and build Singapore into a competitive, information economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: To address that, the PSP's main objective for public housing is to ensure Singaporeans have both affordable housing and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Every Singaporean should be able to have an HDB flat and a basic retirement sum in their CPF without having to downgrade their HDB flat or sell their lease to the Government in retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: By doing this, every Singaporean can be free to realise their full potential in life – and we have the resources to do this.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: PSP's policies are also aimed at giving more choices to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: While ensuring affordability for owner-occupiers, we will aim to maintain a buoyant resale market for Singaporeans who want to monetise their HDB flat and upgrade to private property.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: While we encourage owner-occupation, we also offer more rental flats for Singaporeans at different life stages and circumstances.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: With all this in mind, I will walk the Members through Singaporeans' concerns about public housing before introducing the PSP policy recommendations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The first concern is that affordability has little meaning without accessibility.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government keeps harping on the affordability of BTO flats, but they are in short supply.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: With the waiting times of BTO flats stretching to between five and seven years, compared to between 18 and 24 months during the 1980s, many first-time buyers have no choice but to buy a resale flat.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Hence, overall affordability will depend on the prices of both the BTO and resale flats – and not the BTO flats alone.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Today, resale flats, especially the newer ones, can be as much as 30% higher than BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Resale prices have outpaced wage growth by a large margin over the last three decades.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Singapore has witnessed a streak of 11 consecutive quarters, or nearly three years of price increases in the resale market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Hundreds of resale flats have been transacted above $1 million, with hundreds more being offered on the market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Even though the Government has maintained that BTO prices are not linked to resale prices, Senior Minister of State Sim Ann acknowledged in December last year that the windfall gain from a BTO flat cannot be too large; otherwise, it will be unfair to buyers who were unable to secure a BTO flat.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Indirectly, I take this to mean that while the Government can temporarily slow down the increase in BTO prices when resale prices are surging, like today, BTO prices must eventually keep up with the rise in resale prices over the long term.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Not surprisingly, many in the property market are predicting that the $1 million BTO flat will appear soon.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second concern is, even BTO prices deplete Singaporeans' CPF balances.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government says BTO is affordable because most home buyers need not pay cash to service their monthly mortgages, which can be covered by their CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For the bottom 20% income bracket, it is more than 99%.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Members can also access the handout through the MP@SGPARL app.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The data in the table is based on an HDB advertisement in The Straits Times on 15 January to show that BTO flats are still affordable.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, the advertisement does not show the total cost of home ownership, which is shown in my table.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If you look at the second last row, the number, total cost of home ownership is $592,000.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This is the total cost of home ownership to the buyer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And it is 70% higher than the purchase price.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The drain on CPF savings will be even larger for those who purchase resale flats and also for future generations as BTO prices continue to follow the rise in resale prices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Affordability is not about whether the housing loan can be serviced on a month-to-month basis by CPF savings or not, but by looking at the effect of the total cost of home ownership on the CPF retirement account.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The third concern is lease decay, which has started to threaten the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Even older Singaporeans who have bought their HDB flats at lower prices are exposed to the problems of the current public housing policies – and their problem is lease decay.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We did not need to worry about lease decay in the past, when all flats were young and the Government did not mention it until 2017.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, by 2030, almost half of the HDB flats will be more than 50 years old and the prices of these HDB flats are expected to decline sharply, according to empirical valuation models.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In our local context, limitations on loans and CPF usage will start to affect the prices of flats more than 40 years old, which coincides with the time when retirees want to monetise their flats.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government has promoted the HDB flat as a store of value for retirement and has previously tried to reassure Singaporeans over the lease decay problem with policies such as the Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, as I have said during my Adjournment Motion last month, the Ang Mo Kio Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme (SERS) incident has shown that if the Government uses the same compensation formula as SERS for the older flats in VERS, flat owners will have to put up a significant cash outlay to buy a replacement flat, which they can hardly afford.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It appears that VERS is not a credible solution for the lease decay issue, unless the Government provides further details to prove otherwise.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Without the information, Singaporeans will continue to form ungrounded expectations over VERS and this will disadvantage Singaporeans, especially the lower-income segments, who most need to monetise the flats to supplement their retirement income.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Potential young buyers also want to know whether they can get their CPF savings and accrued interest back when they use them to buy older HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The fourth concern is that a shortage of BTO flats and high resale prices have impacted the total fertility rate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have highlighted this issue since my first Committee of Supply (COS) debate in 2021.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Apart from the newer, longer-term policies we are discussing today, the Government should also take more urgent, short-term measures to help young couples with housing problems instead of relying on limited avenues of help, like the Parenthood Priority Scheme (PPS).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The policy failure today will have dire consequences on our population's structure and economic performance in the future, as young couples will have less incentive to have children due to financial challenges.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My colleague, Ms Hazel Poa, will touch more on this later.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, to address the concerns mentioned above, PSP proposes two policies, the Affordable Homes Scheme and Millennial Apartments Scheme (MAS), with the aim to reset our public housing system to improve affordability and accessibility, strengthen the owner-occupation intent, protect retirement adequacy and reduce social inequality, all of which are embodied in the Motion statement today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I invite Singaporeans to judge the merits of these policies for themselves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The first proposal is Affordable Homes Scheme, which is based on the deferred land cost idea first proposed by Dr Tan Meng Wah in 2013, when he was a research fellow with the Institute of Policy Studies at the National University of Singapore (NUS).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It goes to show that there are many good ideas in the public domain, provided the Government remains open to that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This Affordable Homes Scheme is designed to allow a Singaporean to buy a new flat at a user price, which is equal to the construction cost plus a notional location premium.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If a Singaporean stays in the same flat his entire life, he will only pay the user price.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This user price concept was also suggested by Mr Yeo Lam Keong, the former chief economist of GIC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: At the point of purchase, the land cost for the flat will be made known and recorded with HDB.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If the Singaporean sells his flat in the resale market after the Minimum Occupation Period (MOP), he will have to pay this land cost with accrued interest based on historical mortgage rates into the past reserves, before pocketing the net profit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Thus, he ends up paying the full price of the flat.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We believe owner-occupied public housing is a public good that should be treated as a form of essential public infrastructure, like schools and hospitals, where land cost is not charged because it is treated as state land.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We believe the land used for owner-occupied HDB flats should be treated in the same way as schools and hospitals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Hence, as long as Singaporeans are leasing HDB flats for owner-occupation, they should not have to pay for the land cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They should only pay the land cost when they take the HDB flats to be an investment and sell it for a profit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Affordable Homes Scheme takes care of Singaporeans without hurting the past reserves too much.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: At the lower user price, the buyer will have about $323,000 more in his CPF account, after servicing the housing loan compared to the current BTO pricing system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The buyer will have enough CPF savings to satisfy his basic retirement sum.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, under the Affordable Homes Scheme, HDB will return to its primary objective of providing affordable homes for Singaporeans while CPF will return to its primary objective of providing savings for retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Singaporeans will no longer have to depend on rising property prices to provide for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Every Singaporean will have the Basic Retirement Sum without having to sell their flat or pledge it to the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is also a more equitable way of allocating HDB flats, by lowering the prices of new flats, lower-income Singaporeans will be able to afford flats in better locations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Flats in prime locations will not become enclaves for the upper middle-income class only.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Despite all the abovementioned advantages, the Affordable Homes Scheme will not have a major impact on the nation's fiscal position and reserve accumulation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Currently, about two-thirds of HDB flats are resold after the MOP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Even if this proportion drops with the introduction of the Affordable Homes Scheme, due to the strengthening of the owner-occupation intent, the Government will still be able to recover a substantial part of the deferred land cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Anyway, it is narrow-minded to see the cost of this scheme as a raid on the reserves because affordable housing is an investment in our people for the benefit of the current as well as future generations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And we believe that the interests of current and future generations are not mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If the current generation needs the resources badly, there should be no question of that compromising the interest of the future generation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The best inheritance that we can pass on to our future generation is a current generation that has done well.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Affordable Homes Scheme is aimed at moderating the resale prices, but we are not expecting a precipitous fall in the resale prices because of several reasons.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Second, the market may look further into the horizon and realise that the supply of resale flats will be lower in the future as the owner-occupation intent strengthens.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Thirdly, new sellers will not sell their flats unless the price is high enough for them to earn a profit after paying off the deferred land cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This will reduce the available supply of resale flats and support resale prices in the long term.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This is a good opportunity to resolve both the affordability and lease decay problems at the same time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Our second proposal is the Millennial Apartments Scheme.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The idea is for the Government to keep a large stock of quality rental flats to provide young Singaporeans who desire more space and more independent living with more housing choices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Again, this idea has surfaced from the public domain as a popular demand by the younger generation who desire a greater variety of housing options.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We propose that the main supply of Millennial Apartments come from prime locations near the Central Business District (CBD).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: These locations are currently highly sought after by buyers driven by the profit motive.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But it is more equitable not to sell all the HDB flats in the prime location, but to keep a larger portion of them for rental, so that a broader range of Singaporeans can access these flats.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: These apartments should be attractive because they are close to the workplace, good amenities for families and even vibrant nightlife spots.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Concentrating young Singaporeans together will allow those who are single to have more opportunities to socialise and perhaps, marry; while those are already married will have more time for their families because they live near their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: HDB can also develop a network of shops around these Millennial Apartments to allow a more diverse range of business to operate near the CBD at lower rents.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: With these businesses and a vibrant young population, our CBD can become economically productive day and night.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: While the Government does not acknowledge any problems, the PSP sees the urgent need to reset the public housing policy and has proposed the Affordable Homes Scheme and the Millennial Apartments Scheme as solutions to our public housing malaise.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: On this Valentine's Day, the best Valentine's Day present that this Government can give a young Singaporean couple is an affordable and accessible HDB flat.
